utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Defence wanted to raise a preliminary matter. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning -- good morning, Your Honours. May I just inform you, in accordance with the obligation I took yesterday, we checked P7049 and we have no problem with that, that it be admitted into evidence in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. It's on the record. But the number ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be P7049.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it was in -- it was admitted already but we have now a new format? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks to my colleagues I'm on my feet again. P7049 is admitted into evidence. Then I would like to deal briefly with two matters, and when I start with the second one, the witness can be escorted in the courtroom. But the first one deals with the 92 ter motion for Witness GRM081. On the 12th of December of last year, the Defence filed a motion to admit excerpts of Witness GRM081's prior testimony pursuant to Rule 92 ter. On the 29th of December, the Prosecution filed its response, requesting the admission of the cross-examination from the same prior testimony, along with two associated exhibits. The Prosecution had earlier indicated that this could render the examination of the witness in court unnecessary. However, the Defence has now scheduled its examination-in-chief for two hours, and in all likelihood this may affect the need for cross-examination by the Prosecution because, apparently, other evidence will come in and the Chamber wonders whether, under these circumstances, the Prosecution still wishes to not cross-examine the witness but just tender the testimony given in cross-examination in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution still does not know what the additional evidence exactly would be that would be led in the additional two hours. We have the -- we have the 65 ter summary and the tendered materials to go by. So if there are material -- if there is information as led that is additional that further details of that nature, it would affect the probability of doing some additional cross-examination beyond the tendered cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that you withdraw that request, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record. Then the witness can be escorted in the courtroom while I'll deal with another matter, which is about the Rule 92 ter motion for Dragisa Masal. The Chamber notes that on the 13th of November of last year, the Defence filed a motion tendering 19 associated exhibits with witness Dragisa Masal, and pursuant to the Chamber's guide-lines, the Chamber hereby invites the Defence to consider reducing the number of associated exhibits by, for example, tendering some of these documents with the witness during examination-in-chief. Then, since the witness is escorted in the courtroom, we leave it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to that. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the previous matter raised by the Court, it occurs to me that although Mr. Weber correctly and the court correctly characterised the likelihood of what would happen, we still -- if we were to withdraw the request we eliminate, really, the possibility of no cross-examination. By maintaining the request, should the Court grant it as we would ask, we still keep alive the possibility that the material covered during the two hours does not give rise to further -- so I think in -- out of -- for efficiency reasons we should maintain it and ask the Court to grant it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No one, of course, imposes any duty on the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness. At the same time I think it was all more or less aiming at more or less administratively deal with the evidence of that witness which -- than may be different now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's true. We now revert to a more customary situation, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear for everyone. Good morning, Mr. Trisic. Apologies for not greeting you when you entered the courtroom and continuing with other matters. Mr. Trisic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and the cross-examination will now be resumed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trisic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd just like to remind you of something that you said yesterday with respect to -- or in the context of the discussions we were having over the two documents I showed you which now have the numbers P7221 and P7222. One was the Lazic document and one was the document you recognised as having your signature on the bottom. And talking about these two documents, you said at transcript page 32286: "Our Bratunac Brigade did not need this ammunition. 30-millimetre, 100-millimetre bullets because we did not have these artillery pieces." So now that you've been reminded of that, I just want to have another look at P7221, the Lazic document, and ask you a couple of questions about what you did have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could have P7221 on the screen again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the very last -- the very last type of ammunition referred to in this document is 120-millimetre mortars. The Bratunac Brigade had 120-millimetre mortars; right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just go back one, you also had 82-millimetre mortars in your inventory; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you had 122-millimetre Howitzers in your inventory; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did have 122 Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you had 105-millimetre artillery weapons in your inventory -- or weapons capable of using 105-millimetre artillery shells in your inventory; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So I think that covers -- that covers just about everything on the list that deals with heavier weapons, so we'll just move on now to another topic. I'd just like to ask you briefly about fuel. All right? Now, yesterday we talked about the process for supply and resupply of weapons, and it worked the same way for fuel, didn't it? Your units, Bratunac Brigade units, if they needed fuel, would ask the brigade, you would ask the corps, who would then ask the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, we were a brigade, and I, on behalf of the brigade, asked the corps for fuel. The further procedure doesn't matter. If the corps has fuel, they can provide some to us but they don't have to give the requested quantity. They can give as much as they can, so it can be less than what we had requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just putting the amounts aside for the moment, you've just agreed that that would come through you in your capacity as logistics commander; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so that being the case, perhaps you'll be able to agree with me that the fuel that was requisitioned to evacuate the civilians from Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995 came through you; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one part through us, and another through the corps command. The logistics of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When the fuel provided by the corps logistics group came to your stores in Bratunac, it came through you; right? You were the guy in charge.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If necessary, I will explain how things went on that day, the 12th/13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Just before you launch into any explanation, are you disagreeing with me that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the previous answer indicates, Ms. Edgerton, that the witness disagrees because he says "not necessarily." So, therefore, he at least partly disagrees with you, and I'd like to hear the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For instance, the fuel that arrived from the Drina Corps, that is to say, this truck arrived directly to the parking lot, the Vihor parking, at the entrance into Bratunac. I said that in my statement. The officers from corps logistics directly put that fuel into the buses without us knowing about that. The other part of the fuel that I mentioned that we received, 30 tonnes of diesel fuel, that was put into the Vihor fuel tank. We took care of that, and we put it onto buses, or into buses, and in this way, we justified the consumption of the fuel received.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Trisic, are you saying you didn't know that on the 12th of July, 1995 the Bratunac -- pardon me. The Drina Corps logistics service provided the Bratunac Brigade with 12 -- 11.000 litres of diesel fuel?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right this moment, I cannot recall. I'd need to see the documents. Possibly we requested that fuel. We saw the documents yesterday. So we asked for fuel. Now I'd really have to take a look at the documents. The fuel probably did arrive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a clarification. Mr. Trisic, are you able to tell us how many litres are there in 30 tonnes of diesel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it's around there, sort of, 30.000 litres would be 30 tonnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So since you don't seem to have any recollection without seeing a document, I'll just show you one, Mr. Trisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps we could have a look at 65 ter number 06314.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, this is a fuel receipt dated the 12th of July, 1995 confirming Bratunac Brigade received 6.000 litres of fuel from the Drina Corps Command, and you countersigned it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That can be seen from this material list.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, when you gave evidence just a few minutes ago saying: "The officers from the corps logistics directly put that fuel into the buses without us knowing about that," that wasn't correct. The document shows, at the time, you knew you were receiving large amounts of fuel from the Drina Corps Command; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is part of the fuel that we received in the brigade, this 6.000 litres. I said that the command, the logistics of the Drina Corps, directly I mean, at the Vihor parking lot, at the entrance into Bratunac, got fuel directly into buses and trucks. So it's not the same fuel. This fuel arrived to us in the brigade, and the other part -- well, it was the traffic service of the corps headed by Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic, that did that at the Vihor parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I please have this document as a Prosecution Exhibit, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7223, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move onto another area and forward in time, Mr. Trisic, and I'd like to call up another document in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P1516.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trisic, you've seen this document before, haven't you, when you testified previously at this Tribunal as a Defence witness in the Blagojevic and in the Popovic cases; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's an excerpt from the Bratunac Brigade reports and meetings journal. And if we could go over to the next page, it refers to a meeting dated 16 October 1995, a working meeting of the commander and the Command Staff and the battalion commanders. And when you saw this document during your testimony in the Blagojevic case, you confirmed you attended the meeting. You see your name there in the third line down after the citation to Colonel Blagojevic; don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you were at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since that is what is written there, then I guess I was. It's hard for me to remember that detail; it was such a long time ago. But I accept that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you go a little bit further down in the document to the very bottom line, the very last line in both languages, English and B/C/S, you see Mr. Nikolic reporting that they are currently engaged in tasks issued by the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff and in brackets the word "asanacija" in your language, translated as "hygiene and sanitation measures" in English. So you would agree, then, that on the 16th October 1995, you learned that the Main Staff had directed the reburial of bodies of the men killed at Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Nikolic said that, and there was no comment. Now what was being done, sanitization of the terrain, I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether you learned at that time that this happened. You were not asked for comment. Did you learn that at that time, that the Main Staff had directed, as we see here, the hygiene and sanitation measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found out then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just if I can take that one step further to go back to my original question. You would agree, then, in light of the answer that you've given to His Honour Judge Orie that on this date, 16 October 1995, you learned that the Main Staff had directed the reburial of bodies of the men killed at Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say burial or reburial. In my statement, I said - now was it in Srebrenica? - that's not stated. But in my statement, I said that what happened, happened in the village of Kravica this incident, excessive - how do I put this? - this attack against a guard, and there was gun-fire, and there were casualties, there were dead and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're moving away from the question. The question clearly was that whether, at that meeting, and having looked at the report, whether you then learned that the Main Staff had directed the reburial of bodies. You're not invited to explain what may have caused those persons to die but whether you learned that the Main Staff had directed the reburial of bodies of those men that were killed. Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It just turns out that's what Captain Nikolic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on paper. The question was whether you then learned - and I use the words of the question - that the Main Staff of the VRS had directed the reburial of the bodies. Did you learn that or did you not learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat, I heard that at that meeting from Captain Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the answer, then, is yes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further then, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, you just referred to Kravica. You discussed that yesterday already. I would like to ask you about paragraph 25 of your statement. There you say: "I heard that shots were fired at the Kravica agricultural co-operative." Can you explain that? What did you hear? Did you hear with your own eyes [sic], the shots being fired, or did you hear rumours or stories about the shots fired at Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only heard rumours, as you put it. There were stories about shooting at the Kravica farm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means everything what you know about the incident, as you call it, in Kravica warehouse, that was told by others. It's not what you personally observed or heard with your own ears; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have one or more questions to you. But I'm first inquiring with Ms. Edgerton whether the questions about fuel being provided is in relation to paragraph 23 of the statement, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It wasn't, in particular, but it is certainly a similar subject matter, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In that context, yes. Witness, in paragraph 23 of your statement, you say something about the need to transport civilians. You said you also learned that one fuel tanker from the Drina Corps Command had arrived because the Vihor enterprise pump which was "providing fuel for the buses transporting Muslim civilians from Potocari could not provide all the fuel that was needed." Now, who owned the fuel that was stored in the Vihor enterprise pump? Was it owned by the company, or was it owned by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That fuel tanker was property of the Vihor company. We, as a brigade, we did not have a fuel tank. We did not have a fuel storage, and that's why we used the services of the Vihor transport company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my -- do I then understand that the fuel which was in there was yours, although you used the tank capacity of that company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Records were kept. The fuel in the fuel tank belonged to the -- both to the company and to us, but we knew what quantity belonged to us, and that's what we used. We used only the quantity that belonged to us, and we could easily tell how much we owned by consulting our fuel records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that part of the fuel was yours and part of the fuel was owned by the company. So if I read paragraph 23 now with this additional information, you're telling us that the quantity of fuel at your disposal, though stored in the tanks of the Vihor enterprise, were not sufficient for the transportation of Muslim civilians and that, therefore, the Drina Corps directly delivered additional fuel for those transports. Is that how I have to understand paragraph 23?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The overall transport was organised by the corps. We were there just to assist. We were there to see where fuel could be stored for further use in the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your own fuel was used for that as well, isn't it? For the transport.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. We could not keep our fuel. There was a requirement to transport the population. The Muslim population requested that. A decision was made to transport them. We couldn't then say, We will not give you our fuel, in view of the fact that General Mladic had already agreed on that with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your fuel was used, and in addition to that, directly the corps command provided additional fuel for that transportation. That's, in short, how it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command of the Dutch battalion gave us a fuel tank full of fuel to assist us in order to provide the full quantity of fuel needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have no further questions on this matter. Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in re-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fuel that you received, as you say, from the Dutch battalion, where did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received it in the Vihor transport company, and it was loaded into their fuel tank. I'm talking about the Vihor fuel station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That fuel that you received from the Dutch battalion, was it used to transport the civilian population to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received it by way of assistance which was needed to secure a sufficient quantity of the fuel for this transport to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 06315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, where does this arise, the UNPROFOR fuel? Does that arise from think questions that were put to the witness in cross-examination? He spoke about it, that's clear, but was he asked about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, Your Honours. The last question that was put by the Trial Chamber referred to that, and there was also a -- a question put by the Prosecutor about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, for the last question put by me, I didn't ask about it. The witness spontaneously came up with it. I didn't ask any questions about the UNPROFOR fuel. And we'll check whether a specific question was raised in that respect yesterday by Ms. Edgerton. Perhaps you can assist, Ms. Edgerton. Did you ask specifically about the UNPROFOR fuel? It's my recollection -- it's not my recollection although the witness said something about 30 tonnes and I think 25 tonnes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: While I didn't ask specifically about UNPROFOR fuel, Your Honour, in my submission, there is based on the cross-examination, about fuel which we just went through today with one document, there is some latitude available for a re-direct on issues of fuel. Of course, I will be very attentive as to how far that goes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm specifically talking about UNPROFOR fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I did not have a question about UNPROFOR fuel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither did I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that a question was put yesterday, asking, in general terms, about who provided fuel, and, therefore, you may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You see a document before you. I would kindly ask you to look at the B/C/S text on the left-hand side. The date is 13 July 1995. You can see that in the upper left corner. And where it says military post, you can read 7042. And below that, again the title of the sender, UNHCR Srebrenica, and -- and recipient 7042, Bratunac. First question: Who is 7042 Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the military post of the Light Infantry Brigade in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next column is receipt of diesel fuel D-2. And to the right, quantity received: 30.000 litres. Is this the fuel that was received around that time? And you spoke about that as something that was needed for the transport of the civilian population from Potocari to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the fuel which was received and used for the transport of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like us to look at another document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'll intervene again. First of all, I now carefully verified, you asked a question which I just referred to. It was not the Prosecution. You asked yesterday a question about -- from whom fuel was received. You were the only one. So, therefore, it does not arise specifically out of cross-examination. At the same time, yesterday the witness testified that they received 30 tonnes of diesel fuel from UNPROFOR. Today -- and then the witness said they received 23 and a half thousand litres; 23.300 from UNHCR so you were the only one who raised the matter specifically and now you put to the witness a document which indicates that 30.000 litres were received from UNHCR, not from UNPROFOR. You should have done that yesterday by yourself. Knowing of this document, you should have further examined the witness on whether they had received the 30.000 litres from UNPROFOR or from UNHCR. Now, I'll let you go with the next document, but please keep in mind that the Chamber appreciates orderly proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to call up 65 ter 04164.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, what you can see before you is a document which I would like to discuss with you. Could you please tell us what is this? This is a paper documenting the receipt and issuance of fuels and lubricants?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the issuance of fuel to buses, i.e., vehicles that needed fuel for transport. You can see the registration plate number of the vehicles, and the military post, the date, 14 July 1995, the quantity of the fuel received, and the driver's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the lower right corner, as far as we can see, there is a handwritten name after the text: Order, issuer. Please pay attention to the lower right corner. Try and see if you can read the name of the person who gave the order.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 32, it says Tomislav Basevic and below that, 33, M. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do these names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please speak more directly into the microphone. Perhaps the microphone could be slightly adjusted if the witness looks at his screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I repeat? Under 32 it says Tomislav Basevic. And under 33, M. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do these names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomislav Basevic was a member of the technical service of the Drina Corps. As for Vasiljevic, I can't remember him. I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you see the column where it says "issued, received," under 24, as well as quantities of the fuel issued and received, could you please tell us whether you have any immediate knowledge as to where that fuel was issued to the persons who signed as the recipients of the fuel under 25?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-five? Since Lieutenant-Colonel Tomislav Basevic signed this, this fuel was not issued from the fuel tank of the Vihor company. It was probably issued at the parking lot of the Vihor company where the fuel tank of the Drina Corps was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender these two documents, 65 ter 06315 and 65 ter 04164 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 06315 will be Exhibit D940. And 65 ter number 04164 will be Exhibit D941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence. Witness, could you tell us what military post code 7469 stands for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was a question by the Presiding Judge for you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You said military post 7469. It's neither here nor there. These -- or, rather, this is proof that buses and vehicles came from various military posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you simply whether you know what military post code 7469 stands for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That the vehicle is property of that military post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is that military post? That's my question. Not whether the vehicle is owned by ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I leave it to that, but you asked the witness about what one could conclude from column 25. The witness then said that on the basis of what he saw under 32, he drew some conclusions, and you left it to that. Therefore, he's dealing with a matter not the matter you raised, and I just draw your attention to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, you were shown a document which I would like to call up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1516.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report or, rather, a copy of the minutes dated 16 October of the Bratunac Brigade. Do you have any recollection whether, on that occasion, Momir Nikolic described the sanitization activity which was under way, very specifically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection, no specific recollection. That was such a long time ago that it is impossible to remember specific details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to your military education, is it of the kind that you would be able to tell the Trial Chamber how do you define the term sanitization or hygiene measure -- measures of the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to define it. It would be the cleaning of the area. Something of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether in the area where the 28th Division column passed and where combat had taken place, there was a need to, as you say, clean the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your brigade have any particular engagement with regard to the cleaning of the areas that you would know of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade was not engaged in that way. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me finish with the question: Did you personally have an occasion to see any document which originated from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and that dealt with the obligation of any unit to be engaged in the sanitization of the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have occasion to see any such document originating from a superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, thank you for your answers on behalf of the Defence of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, which have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Moloto has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, you were being asked by Mr. Stojanovic about whether the 28th Division column passed and where combat had take place. Now, in relation to this document that's on the screen, do you know whether the 28th Division was anywhere around there in October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In October 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where it could have been. It wasn't in our area, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in this meeting of the 16th of October 1995, Nikolic is talking about sanitation that you have just been tasked to do; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't have information as to where this was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where it was carried out. I'm saying you have agreed that this statement by Nikolic on the 16th of October in the meeting is referring to you -- your -- your people being tasked to do some sanitation in October of 1995. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That we were carrying out the sanitization of the terrain? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you carried out the sanitation. I am saying you are being told in this meeting by Nikolic that the Main Staff of the VRS has tasked your unit with sanitation. He's telling you this statement on the 16th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not carry out sanitization of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I stop you. I stop you there. Please listen to my question. I'm not asking you whether you carried out sanitation. I'm saying you are having a meeting on the 16th of October, you're being told that the VRS Main Staff has given an order that you take -- undertake sanitation measures. This is on the 16th of October. And on that date, you're saying the 28th Division was nowhere in your area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud. No speaking aloud, Mr. Mladic. No speaking aloud. You may consult with counsel at inaudible volume. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. Are you going to answer my question? If you don't want to answer or if you don't know -- in fact, you cannot not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know, Your Honour, Judge, how to express myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't know how to express yourself, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I apologise for what might be construed as an interruption. I'm just noting the time. Just for purposes of scheduling, and I wanted to let Your Honours know based on what we just heard, I would have another seven to ten minutes' worth of questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will do that after the break. I would like, however, to put one other question to the witness before the break. Witness, Captain Nikolic, was he within your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was in our brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we read in this document that Captain Nikolic says, We are currently engaged in tasks issued by the ... Main Staff on sanitacija. You emphasised several times that your brigade was not involved in that at all. Do you have any explanation why Captain Nikolic is recorded as saying, We are engaged; whereas, you say the brigade was not engaged. Do you have an explanation for why your testimony squarely contradicts what we see in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assert that as assistant commander for logistics in the Bratunac Brigade, I did not know, I was not informed that this sanitization of the terrain was being carried out. Captain Nikolic worked in the intelligence security service, so I cannot decipher what it was that he meant, that he would be doing it, somebody else would be doing it, but as assistant commander for logistics of the brigade did not carry out sanitization, and I was not aware of this being sanitization.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hear that. But you said the brigade was not involved. But what you're telling us now is that you have no information whatsoever about an involvement of the brigade, although, by not knowing, you cannot exclude that the brigade was involved. Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, as assistant commander for logistics, did not have any vehicles and did not provide any vehicles for these obligations. Not fuel either or personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not involved; that's understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break. Ms. Edgerton, you'll have a few more minutes after the break. You may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. In order to avoid whatever confusion, when earlier today, P7049 was admitted into evidence, it was Rule 65 ter 14008a that was admitted, and not the 65 ter document that was previously uploaded and for which the number P7049 was reserved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Further cross-examination by Ms. Edgerton:

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, I want to ask you some further questions based on the answers you've just given to my colleague. Just to see if we can tie up one brief matter with respect to D941, you were asked a question, in fact, by Their Honours about a certain military post number and it was a VP 7469. That's actually, in fact, that's the military post number for the Zvornik Brigade isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe it or not, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And -- all right. That's fine. And we'll go on to the next larger area I want to deal with. Just before the break, you effectively told Their Honours that this asanacija -- that did you not know and were not informed about the asanacija of the terrain before the 16th of October; right? That's your position you didn't know about it because that what's you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Good. So I want to ask you some questions about that. First of all, I'd like you to confirm the evidence that you gave in the Popovic cases during your examination-in-chief about the bodies from Kravica. And I can even show it to you, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 32290. We can go directly to e-court, page 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to try and speed things up, I want to show it to you. Now I'm going read this to you. The question at line 4: "And tell me" -- this is to Mr. Lazarevic: "Q. And tell me whether if at any point in time you learned that the bodies of those killed in the Kravica farmer's co-operative were buried in a grave in the village of Glogova?" Your answer is: "Yes. I did have that information a day or two afterwards. I found out from my friend who was engaged on that task that the burial was completed of those who were killed in the Glogova village section." So you stand by that evidence? You gave it in your examination-in-chief as a Defence witness in Popovic. You stand by that evidence; right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in the month of July. A friend of mine who worked -- who was engaged on this sanitization said that to me. That was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So -- so my question is: You stand by the evidence you gave in the Popovic case; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what's the name of the friend who was engaged on that task? In the burial.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a friend of mine who worked in civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked the name. Could you please tell us who it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name, Dragan. Dragan Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I just want to remind you for a couple of minutes of what was going on in September and October 1995 in the area of responsibility of your brigade and surrounding. What was going on was that thousands of Bosnian Muslim men who were -- had been killed at Branjevo, in Kozluk, Petkovci Dam, Orahovac and Kravica were moved from mass graves in Bratunac and Zvornik to other mass graves in Bratunac and Zvornik, and that included over a thousand people who had been buried in Glogova. So I'm not going -- I'm going to get to my question in a minute but I just wanted to remind you of that evidence. And I want to read to you what one witness who didn't testify in this trial but was interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in November 2001 said about what was going on, and then I will ask you a question. That witness said, in the context of that operation: "There were lorries transporting bodies for hours. Even children along the side of the road were finding arms and legs. I do know that," he said that. And then he was asked: "Did you see that? And he answered: "I didn't see that, but I could smell it. I could smell the stench." And then he was asked: "Where were you when you could smell it? "I was in the flat," he replied. And then the question was: "In Bratunac?" And he said: "Yes." And then he continued, saying: "I know what the stench was when I smelled it because it's a very characteristic smell of a human body which is decomposing." Now, here's my question, Mr. Trisic: I'd like you to explain how it's possible when you had an apartment on the main road in Bratunac, 50 metres across the street from the Hotel Fontana, that you didn't know about the decomposing bodies that were being transferred throughout the municipality at that time? Because everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said and I maintain that, regardless of where I live, I didn't feel that or see that. Most of the time I was at the brigade command so I still maintain that I did not see that or feel that, what you said, this unpleasant smell.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Witness, Mr. Trisic, this concludes your evidence in this case. We'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague - it's a long journey - and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, were put to you by the parties and were put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Mr. McCloskey and I will now take our leave with Your Honours' permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the Prosecution is still represented in this courtroom, Mr. Weber and Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're on course for getting the response regarding the extension of time for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you said yesterday tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, so that still is within your time estimate. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. The next witness would be General Dragisa Masal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning again. The Prosecution just had one matter before the witness takes the stand. The Prosecution requests that this witness get a 90(E) admonishment, actually before he begins his testimony based on the contents of the statement. A specific example would be paragraph 28. I don't know if the Defence has any view on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As Your Honours know, we have always left that to the discretion of the Chamber to determine whether 90(E) is appropriate or not. We don't have an objection to the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, as you know, the Chamber not knowing what questions to be put to the witness always leaves it to the parties to consider whether it would be appropriate or not, and apparently you do not challenge this provisional judgement that it would be appropriate by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Masal. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Masal, before the Defence will start its examination, I'd like to draw your attention to Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and I'll read it for you. "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." In short, if you feel that an answer might tend to incriminate yourself, a truthful answer, you may address me and ask to be relieved from answering that question. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you know that you're -- you've just given the solemn declaration. You know that if you answer a question it should be a truthful answer. You'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic, and you'll find Mr. Ivetic standing to your left. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With the assistance of the usher if we could have a hard copy of the statement first shown to Prosecution counsel and eventually given to the witness. It will help us as we get to that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, General. Can I ask you to first state your full name, first and last, for the purposes of entering the same into our record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Good day, Your Honours. Good day to all present here in this courtroom. I am Dragisa Masal, born on the 20th of November, 1951, in the village of Vardiste, municipality of Visegrad, Republika Srpska. I have completed elementary school and high school. That I completed in the place where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think we need that additional information at this moment. Did you have occasion to give a witness statement to the members of General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, usually it goes better if you have the band on top of your head rather than behind. At the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up in e-court 1D1642.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you have been given a hard copy in front of you. You can either follow on the monitor or on that hard copy. And I'd like to first ask you if you recognise the handwritten signature on the first page of the same, if you could tell us whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the signature. It is my very own.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the last page of the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, there is also a handwritten signature on this page. Could you identify for us the author of that signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Likewise, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there's a handwritten date on here that looks like the 28th of July, 2014. Does that date match your recollection of the date that you would have signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And subsequent to signing this statement, did you have occasion to read the same, to see if everything is written correctly or if corrections are needed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes, I read the text, and I spotted certain technical errors. In essence, they do not alter the sense of my statement. However, there are technical errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go through some of those with you now. If we could first turn to page 2 in both versions and focus on paragraph number 2, and is there any correction that you need to make in relation to the posts that you held before the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, line 2, the words "battalion commander" should be deleted because I was not a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this same paragraph, are there any corrections needed to the last part of the paragraph relating to your position after the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: In the last line of the same paragraph, it reads: "...sector chief at the newly formed... staff." This should read: At the newly formed General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now, sir, in relation to the first sentence in this paragraph, I note that the English translation says: "Before the war started in the former Yugoslavia, I held ..." Can you -- whereas the Serbian seems to have "former JNA" instead of "former Yugoslavia." Can you confirm which -- which is the appropriate entry for this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: In my view, it should say: "Before the beginning of the war, in the former JNA, I discharged duties." This means that I discharged certain duties in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now on page 7 in the Serbian, page 8 in the English, and paragraph 16, what correction do you have in relation to the information that you had received from Gorazde which is reflected in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: In line 2 of this paragraph, it says that the Muslim civilian population in Gorazde, and so on and so forth. This should be replaced by the following: "The Serbian civilian population in Gorazde was used for military purpose, i.e. -- purposes, i.e., for performing some works in the rear."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now in relation to paragraph 17 on the same page, what correction did you wish to inform us of in relation to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Please bear with me. In line 4: "The Muslim forces are kept under permanent blockade in order to prevent their insertion ..." This is how the paragraph should read. At the moment the word "to prevent" is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can turn to page 8 in the Serbian, page 10 in the English and focus on paragraph 21, and now that we have it on the screen, do you have a correction in relation to what is contained in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Please bear with me. In line 1 of this paragraph, it says: "I was often briefed through regular combat reports," there is a grammatical error in B/C/S. In B/C/S, the word "through" is used improperly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you clarify how it -- how should it read now? What is the correct wording?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat, sir, the correct wording in B/C/S, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I shall try to explain. "I was often briefed via regular combat reports" or "through regular combat reports." In the current B/C/S version, the word used is "from regular combat reports." But that would mean that a combat report is a living being that submits certain information to me. However, a combat report is a document which somebody sends and that somebody is a subordinated command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the English version is correct and that there may be a grammatical error in the original but that doesn't create any confusion at this moment, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at page 11 in the English, page 10 in the Serbian and look at paragraph 23. I note, sir, that in the second-to-last sentence of English the word "General Staff" appears but in the Serbian we only see the initials GS. Can you tell us to what entity the GS refers to as contained in your Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the transcript reflects on line 10 of this page that we're looking at paragraph 23. However, I believe it may be paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Nope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 23, fourth line from the bottom in English, talks about General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I missed that then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's apparently what are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can turn to page 13 in the Serbian and page 14 in the English, and focus on paragraph 28 of your statement, what correction do you have that you wish to bring to our attention in relation to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is thinking about it, Mr. Ivetic, for the previous correction, "the failed to be replaced" by "not include," is that in the B/C/S also incorrectly phrased?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is it just the English version that does not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought it was just the English, but I'll have to check just to be sure. I might have to go back to that one because I don't see that it's actually clear from the answer of the witness whether it's a grammatical error or a substantive correction. I will go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could first finish up with paragraph 28, sir, what is the correction that you had in there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: I'm still looking. I would need to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can assist, the -- the third line of 28 --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- in the Serbian version, that reads as follows: "Gives basic tasks to the units which are carrying out orders."

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What -- what, if any, corrections are there to that phrase in paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: "Gives basic tasks to the units which are carrying out orders." It should read: "Gives basic tasks to the units which are carrying out the operation," or "which are engaged in combat."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can go back to page 13 in the English, page 11 in the Serbian, the paragraph in question is paragraph 25, and I would ask you again to explain for us what precisely is the correction that you indicated should be in the last part of that paragraph, the last -- was it the last line? I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be better to read the correct version of the full last sentence. Sometimes subordinate units ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's an excellent suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you read how the last sentence of paragraph 25 ought to read, including your correction.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes. "Sometimes subordinated units of the brigade reported to the corps about a particular event, incident and the like, and the corps would then not inform the Main Staff about that." The first part of the sentence is correct. Brigade does, indeed, report to the corps. According to the same analogy, i.e., according to the military terminology the corps command should inform the Main Staff. The principle in military subordination implies that the subordinate unit reports to the superior unit whereas a superior unit informs the subordinate unit. The error arises from military terminology and the notion of military subordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And how should the sentence read now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just read out the correct verse of the sentence. It should read: "And the corps would then fail to include this in its information to the General Staff." Not in its report to the General Staff, but in its information to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do we then have to understand that they sometimes do not include it in the information to the Main Staff, or that it's never included, or is it that just it could be left out sometimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is only about terminology. The penultimate word, "a subordinate" cannot send information to the superior. A subordinate unit reports to the superior unit. That is the difference in terminology between the word "informs," on the one hand, and "reports" on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, any further communication with the public gallery will result in you being removed from the courtroom. Is that clear to you? You better turn in ... and address ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I leave it to you to clarify the matter, but to say that it -- of course, this Chamber is not only interested in terminology, this Chamber is interested in substance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell you that at issue is the difference between two Serbian words, if I can find the Serbian version in front of me, which the witness has explained in Serbian and we've gotten the translation of. He has identified the second to last word in that sentence that currently in the B/C/S version reads "obavesti" and is indicating that it should read "izvesti." But we're not getting translation of either, so that doesn't really help the English speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly does not. Of course, what the Chamber is interested in is what information reached the higher-up levels. I mean, that's basically what I think is important for us to know and whether sometimes the format or the form in which that happened may be relevant, important, but most of all is what information reached the higher levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that I believe is contained in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both versions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on. If you feel that further clarification is needed, you'll certainly find a way to find that in your further examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 5 in both versions, we had uploaded, I believe yesterday, a new English translation from CLSS to correct -- there was a missing paragraph that was contained in the Serbian signed original that was not in -- a subparagraph, I should say, that was not in the English translation, and in uploading that translation that we had from CLSS, I have been advised and I have now confirmed that there is now in paragraph 11 the first sentence in the English is not in the signed original. We will -- the Prosecution is aware of this; they're the ones who pointed it out to me. Therefore we will have to correct the English translation and upload a new translation and I wanted to bring that to everyone's attention and put it on the record so that we will not be tendering the document after the 92 ter procedure is done, we'll be tendering it to be marked for identification once we finished the remaining aspects of that procedure. But, of course, this is something that is not -- there's no correction to be made to the original. It's just the translation that has that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The translation contains lines which are not -- do not appear in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Not lines, a sentence, the first sentence in 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, that would trigger a few questions on how possibly can lines which do not appear in the original suddenly appear on a translation. Has the original, as signed, been submitted to CLSS?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It has Your Honour and this is -- both the translation that was missing the second subparagraph in paragraph 27 and this one are CLSS translations, is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The English version now contains a long first sentence which was not contained in the attachment to the 92 ter motion. What I see now on the screen is -- in the English version, I think complete in comparison to the previously submitted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ivetic, could you give us -- we'll reserve a number for the document. Could you inform the Chamber in detail about what happened with an original which was partly not translated then and other lines were apparently added in the translation which really comes as a surprise. Because the interpreter -- the translator would then have invented new text and that really is so surprising that the Chamber would like to know how this happened. We have your initial explanation on the screen now. We'll reserve a number for the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We haven't yet done the 92 ter procedure in full. It's too early to reserve a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reserving a number for admission I would agree, but I think it would be good to seek attestations. Of course, at the same time, Mr. Ivetic, the issue is attestation to what exactly, because we seek an attestation to what the witness has read and we have to know exactly what he reviewed whether that was the version that is now on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is. In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He obviously did not read the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand that. But just to be sure that the questions that were raised a minute ago ask for great accuracy in this respect. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just so we have a clear record, the Prosecution's position is that the first sentence should be redacted up to the word or the phrase "civilian population to," then the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is in the English you would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed with the attestations and ... take -- take the B/C/S as the basis for it, if that's what the witness reviewed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, apart from these corrections we've gone through today, do you stand by the remainder of your statement as signed in the Serbian language as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you questions today on the same topics as in your written statement, would your answers today be, in substance -- be the same in substance as written in that statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, since you have taken the solemn declaration today to tell the truth, does that mean that your statement is truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours we would ask for the 1D01642 to be marked for identification pending resolution of the transcript. Pardon me, of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D942, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Mr. Weber, anticipating that we finally will resolve the matter, are there any objections against admission if everything has been sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour, no, there wouldn't be with that redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We also have a reduced number of associated exhibits that we would tender at this time. The number is 14. And the document identified in the statement as 1D03014 is already in evidence as P01977. And the document referred to in the statement that we identified as 65 ter number 19198 is already in evidence as P02006. At this point I don't know if you want me to read the 65 ter numbers of the documents that remain or if you want to do that by written means after the examination. I can do either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be best that Mr. Registrar prepares a list of the remaining and perhaps already provisionally assigns numbers to it. But, Mr. Weber, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's my understanding that the rest of the associated exhibits are being tendered. We have no objection with that so I just want to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There's one more, I think. Also, there is one that is identified as 65 ter number 08977 which received a number P00780 and was marked not admitted. And I believe that's the one that counsel and I talked about before the witness started and we would tender it at this time since now two witnesses have talked about that document. It was previously marked not admitted as P00780.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct. It's an associated exhibit now to two different statements of witnesses in this case. Simply the Chamber is going to need the document to understand what the separate witnesses are saying about the material. It should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You're recorded as saying, "not be admitted."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It should be -- we would like. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. And that is our correct position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you tender it now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as well, and it already been assigned that number. We are talking about 65 ter 08977 which was -- had already P780.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.text: And now since both parties are seeking admission of that ...
